sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About How Cancer Vaccines Work
sectionToMerge.intro: Cancer vaccines are an evolving form of immunotherapy that helps the immune system recognise and fight cancer cells. These FAQs explain how they work, who may benefit, and what patients should know about their types, safety, and access.

items.a: A cancer vaccine is a type of immunotherapy that trains the immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells. Unlike vaccines that prevent infections, most cancer vaccines are designed to treat existing disease by helping immune cells identify tumour-specific markers called antigens. They may be considered for selected patients depending on cancer type, stage, and biomarker profile, and are usually given alongside other treatments after review by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: What is the difference between preventive and treatment cancer vaccines?
items.a: Preventive cancer vaccines stop cancers linked to certain infections, while therapeutic vaccines treat cancer that already exists. Preventive vaccines, such as those against HPV or hepatitis B, lower the risk of cervical, head and neck, and liver cancers. Therapeutic vaccines aim to shrink tumours or reduce recurrence by stimulating an immune attack. Whether either option is suitable depends on cancer type, stage, and specialist review by a qualified oncology team.

groups.title: How They Work, Eligibility, and Safety

items.a: Cancer vaccines work by exposing the immune system to tumour antigens so it can identify and destroy cancer cells carrying those markers. The vaccine may use proteins, genetic material such as mRNA, or modified cells to prompt a targeted immune response. Once activated, T cells and antibodies can seek out matching cancer cells in the body. The strength of this response varies between patients and depends on individual and tumour factors.

items.q: What are the different types of cancer vaccines?
items.a: The main types of cancer vaccines include tumour cell, protein or peptide, dendritic cell, and genetic vaccines using DNA or mRNA. Dendritic cell vaccines are made using a patient's own immune cells, while mRNA and peptide vaccines may be tailored to tumour-specific mutations, sometimes called personalised or neoantigen vaccines. The most appropriate option depends on cancer type, biomarkers, and availability, and many newer types remain under investigation in clinical trials.

items.q: Who may be eligible for a cancer vaccine?
items.a: Eligibility for a cancer vaccine depends on cancer type, stage, biomarker profile, previous treatment, and overall health. Some therapeutic vaccines are approved for specific cancers such as prostate cancer or melanoma, while many others are available only through clinical trials. A specialist reviews pathology, imaging, and molecular test results before recommending this approach. Final treatment decisions should be made by the treating medical team after full assessment of the individual patient.

Cancer vaccines are generally well tolerated, but they can cause side effects that should be discussed with your oncology team. Common reactions include fever, fatigue, chills, and soreness or swelling at the injection site, which are usually mild and temporary. Less often, stronger immune reactions may occur and require monitoring. Because responses vary between patients, safety depends on the specific vaccine, cancer type, and overall health, and no treatment is completely risk-free.

items.q: How much do cancer vaccines cost and are they widely available?
items.a: The cost and availability of cancer vaccines vary widely because most therapeutic vaccines are still offered through clinical trials or specialised centres. A few approved vaccines exist for specific cancers, but personalised options can be expensive and are not available everywhere. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, stage, tests, treatment protocol, and length of stay. Access also depends on eligibility, medical review, and, for trials, investigator assessment.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with cancer vaccines?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health.
